idiom_name: legacy interface implementation delegating to the new service
implementation_notes: The window is a class that implements the frozen legacy interface and forwards every method to the modernized service, with the mapping kept in one place; if the boundary is JSON or XML, the serializer configuration pins the old wire shape, and @Deprecated(forRemoval = true) on the frozen interface marks it as legacy-only so the first new caller gets a warning. The annotation is the JDK's own vocabulary for this situation - 'discouraged from using', optionally 'subject to removal in a future version' - which is exactly the lifetime a window should advertise. The hand-written adapter is still justified when the legacy interface is a real binary contract (an RMI/IDL surface, a published jar) or when its methods need genuine argument juggling; for wide interfaces with uniform mapping, java.lang.reflect.Proxy synthesises the window instead of hand-writing every stub.
pitfalls: Checked exceptions are part of the contract: changing which ones escape, or replacing them with newer types, breaks callers as surely as changing a signature.
Thread-safety expectations carry over: if the legacy interface promised to be thread-safe, the window must remain stateless or synchronise, whatever the new core guarantees.
An adapter that mirrors the new API back into the old shape (rather than mapping to the legacy one) silently re-freezes the new model as the contract.

variants.name: Synthesised window via java.lang.reflect.Proxy
variants.implementation_notes: For a wide or generated legacy interface, Proxy.newProxyInstance(Foo.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{Foo.class}, handler) creates a class at runtime that implements exactly the listed interfaces and dispatches every call into one invocation handler, so the window becomes a mapping table instead of dozens of stubs. The javadoc fixes the sharp edges the handler must respect: a proxy class is final and implements only interfaces, duplicate methods resolve to the foremost interface that declares them, and a checked exception thrown outside the method's declared set surfaces as an UndeclaredThrowableException. Choose it when the mapping is uniform and the interface is broad; prefer the plain adapter when the legacy calls need individual handling.
pitfalls: Only interfaces can be proxied: a legacy class contract still needs a hand-written adapter (or a bytecode library).
Mirroring methods generically inside the handler reintroduces the legacy shape into the new API; keep the mapping table explicit and total.
Reflective dispatch fails at runtime, not at compile time, so the contract fixtures are the only thing protecting the client.
